1:
The householder Anāthapiṇḍika brought five hundred friends who followed other teachers
to Jetavana, carrying flowers, perfumes and offerings.
2: Hearing the Buddha’s teaching, the friends gained faith. They left their old teachers and went for refuge to the Buddha.
3: But when the Buddha went away to Rājagaha, they broke their refuge and went back to their old teachers.
4:
When the Buddha returned, Anāthapiṇḍika brought them again. Asked whether they had broken their refuge, they could not deny it;
at Anāthapiṇḍika’s request the Buddha told a story of the past.
5: Long ago in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born a merchant. He and a foolish merchant of the same city each loaded five hundred carts.
6:
The Bodhisatta said, “If we travel together, water, firewood and fodder will run short.
Will you go first or later?” The foolish merchant chose to go first.
7:
The foolish merchant thought, “If I go first, the road, the grass and the water will be fresh,
and I can set my own prices.”
9: At the edge of a waterless desert sixty yojanas wide, the foolish merchant filled great jars with water and loaded them on the carts.
10: In the middle of the desert a man-eating yakkha came toward them, dripping wet, riding a splendid carriage drawn by white oxen.
11:
Meaning to weaken them and then devour them, the yakkha tempted them:
“Up ahead it always rains, and the pools are full of lotuses. Throw away your heavy water and travel light.”
12:
In his foolishness the merchant believed him and had all the water poured out.
The yakkha soon passed out of sight.
13: But however far they went, there was not a drop of water. Men and oxen staggered, parched with thirst.
14:
At sunset the company drew the carts into a circle, but there was no water for the oxen and no food for the men;
they collapsed into sleep, worn out by thirst and hunger.
15: That night the yakkhas came out of the darkness and devoured all the sleeping men and oxen.
16: In the morning only the loaded carts remained, and white bones lay scattered on the sand.
17:
A month and a half later, the Bodhisatta set out with five hundred carts of his own,
every jar filled with water.
18: The Bodhisatta told his men, “Do not use even a handful of water without my leave. There are poisonous trees in the desert, so eat no leaf, flower or fruit without asking me.”
19: In the middle of the desert the same yakkha came again in his ox-drawn carriage. The Bodhisatta raised his hand and halted the carts.
20: Seeing the yakkha’s red eyes, his fearless bearing, and that he cast no shadow, the Bodhisatta knew he was not a human being.
21: The yakkha urged them to throw the water away, but the Bodhisatta refused: “We will throw it away when we see water.” The yakkha left.
22: When his men begged to throw the water away, the Bodhisatta asked, “Has anyone seen a rain cloud?” The sky was perfectly clear.
23: “Has anyone felt a damp wind, seen lightning, or heard thunder?” No one had. “Those were not men. They were yakkhas.”
24:
The Bodhisatta reasoned, “The caravan ahead must surely have been devoured by yakkhas.”
And on the way they came upon abandoned carts and white bones.
25:
The Bodhisatta had his cheap goods unloaded and the valuable goods
from the abandoned carts loaded instead. He also exchanged weak carts for strong ones.
26: At nightfall the Bodhisatta drew the carts into a circle like a fence, and let the men and oxen rest inside.
27: The Bodhisatta himself led the guard. Sword in hand, he stood watch through the three watches of the night until dawn.
28: Having crossed the desert, the Bodhisatta sold his goods for two and three times their value.
29: The Bodhisatta brought his company safely back to Bārāṇasī without losing a single man.
30:
When the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths, the five hundred listeners attained stream-entry.
“The foolish merchant then was Devadatta, and the wise merchant was I myself.”
